title: CLIL in Full — Planning a Content Unit

points.h: Selecting Content for a Full Unit
pts: A full CLIL unit needs content substantial enough to sustain several lessons of genuine cognitive engagement.
Content should connect meaningfully to the wider curriculum, not stand alone as a novelty within the language course.
This extends Unit 37's light-touch content selection into a more demanding, sustained choice.

v: The subject syllabus for one class; a five-question filter

items: List three possible topics from the subject syllabus for next term.
Rate each topic from 1 to 3 on five questions (see model language).
Choose the topic with the highest total, unless a strong reason overrides it.
Check with the subject teacher that the unit will teach, not merely repeat, part of the subject syllabus.
Write the unit’s three main content outcomes.
Where no subject colleague is available, use the state textbook and its learning outcomes as the reference.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Is there enough substance for six lessons of real thinking?
Does it connect to the subject curriculum this term?
Is it relevant to learners’ lives and locality?
Can it be taught with visuals, objects or data rather than long texts?
Is the language load manageable with scaffolding?

blocks.x: Result: Water management in our district scores 14 out of 15. It links to the syllabus on natural resources, uses local data, and supports cause and effect and recommendation. A single-lesson topic such as ‘the water cycle’ (Unit 26) would not sustain six lessons.

body: Purpose: to show content selection for a full unit. Content: several topic cards dropping into a funnel with five labelled filter layers; one card emerges at the bottom. Style: clean, simple. Board version: a funnel shape with five lines across it.

items: Google Sheets (free) to score topics jointly.

blocks.x: A five-row table in the staff planning register.

points.h: Planning With the 4Cs at Unit Scale
pts: Map content, communication, cognition and culture demands across every lesson in the unit, not just the unit as a whole.
This reveals uneven demand across the unit early — a lesson accidentally overloading cognition and language simultaneously, for instance.
This is the 4Cs framework from Unit 37, applied with unit-level planning discipline.

v: A grid with six columns (lessons) and four rows (the 4Cs)

items: Write a one-line aim for each of the six lessons.
Fill each cell: the content, communication, cognitive demand and cultural or community dimension of that lesson.
Mark each cell H, M or L for demand.
Look for lessons where cognition and language are both high, and redistribute where possible.
Check that the cognitive demand rises across the unit, from remembering and understanding towards evaluating and creating (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001).
Colour-code the grid so that uneven demand is visible at a glance.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Part of the grid (written for this book):

lines: L1 Where our water comes from: content: sources; communication: naming, describing (L); cognition: remember (L); culture: local wells and lakes.
L3 Why the lake is shrinking: content: causes; communication: cause and effect (H); cognition: analyse (H); culture: interview elders.
L6 Our proposal: content: solutions; communication: recommending, persuading (H); cognition: evaluate, create (H); culture: presenting to the panchayat or ward committee.

blocks.x: Lesson 3 was overloaded, with a new text, a new language function and analysis all at once. The planners moved the interviews to Lesson 2 so that learners met the causes informally before analysing them.

body: Purpose: to show uneven demand across a unit. Content: a six-by-four grid with cells shaded light to dark; one column is conspicuously dark and circled. Style: heat-map style with labels as well as shading. Board version: a grid with H, M and L letters.

items: Google Sheets (free) with conditional formatting for demand levels.

blocks.x: A grid on chart paper with coloured dots.

pts: Plan a deliberate scaffolding arc across the unit — heavier support early, more independence as content and language both become familiar.
Visual organisers, graphic scaffolds and language frames should evolve across the unit, not repeat identically each lesson.
This connects to Unit 15's differentiation principles, applied specifically to the compounded content-language demand of CLIL.

v: Graphic organizers and sentence frames at three levels of support

items: In Lesson 1, give a labelled diagram, a word bank and full sentence frames.
In Lessons 2–3, give a partly completed graphic organizer and sentence starters only.
In Lessons 4–5, give headings only; learners choose their own organizer.
In Lesson 6, learners plan and present with no frame, using a checklist.
Keep earlier scaffolds available on the wall for learners who need them.
Let learners choose their level of scaffold at each stage, with the teacher advising.
Support: learners keep the full frames longer and add home-language notes.
Challenge: learners design a graphic organizer for others to use.

blocks.x: The same function at three stages (written for this book):

lines: Lesson 2 frame: The lake is shrinking because ______. This means that ______.
Lesson 4 starter: One reason for… / As a result…
Lesson 6: learners explain causes and effects in their own words, with a checklist: Did I give a reason? Did I show the result?
S1: Ma’am, I don’t need the frame now. I can say ‘As a result, the wells have become dry.’

blocks.x: Gibbons (2015) describes scaffolding as temporary support that is withdrawn as learners gain control, and the fade should be planned across the unit, not repeated identically in every lesson. This applies the differentiation principles of Unit 15 to the double demand of CLIL.

body: Purpose: to show a planned scaffolding arc. Content: a building under construction shown at three stages; the scaffolding is full in the first, partial in the second and gone in the third. Style: simple architectural sketch. Board version: three rectangles with fewer lines around each.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for graphic organizers.

blocks.x: Organizers drawn in notebooks from a model on the board.

points.h: Language of, For, and Through Learning at Scale
pts: Map subject-specific vocabulary (language of), classroom task language (language for), and anticipated emergent language (language through) for the whole unit.
This turns Unit 37's three-layer framework from an occasional planning note into a full unit-planning tool.
Anticipating language through learning is necessarily provisional — build in flexibility to respond to what actually emerges.

v: 40 minutes to plan; 5 minutes per lesson
A three-column map; a class ‘new language’ chart

items: For the whole unit, list language of learning: the key subject terms and structures.
List language for learning: what learners need to do the tasks, such as asking for data or agreeing in groups.
Predict some language through learning: what may emerge as learners work.
During the unit, keep a class chart on which learners add useful language they needed and discovered.
At the end of each lesson, spend five minutes reviewing the chart and adding to the map.
Learners keep a personal glossary with a home-language column.
Support: key terms with pictures and home-language equivalents.
Challenge: learners write definitions in their own words.

blocks.x: A language map for the water unit (written for this book):

lines: Of: groundwater, recharge, borewell, catchment, encroachment; the passive (is recharged, was encroached).
For: Can you read the figure for 2010? / I think it’s because… / Let’s check the graph.
Through (emerged): water table, tanker mafia, rainwater harvesting pit.
S1: My grandfather called it ‘kere’. What is it in English?
T: A lake, or a tank. In Karnataka, many man-made lakes are called tanks. Let’s add both to the chart.

blocks.x: Language through learning cannot be fully planned; the chart makes it visible and teachable (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).

body: Purpose: to show the language triptych at unit scale. Content: three stacked transparent layers labelled ‘of’, ‘for’ and ‘through’, the top one with blank spaces marked ‘to be discovered’. Style: clean, layered. Board version: three columns with headings.

items: Quizlet (free basic plan) for a class set of key terms. [VERIFY current free features]

blocks.x: A chart on the classroom wall that grows across the unit.

pts: Track content and language assessment as separate, parallel strands across the unit, not just within a single task.
This extends Unit 37's dual-rubric principle to a cumulative, unit-level assessment picture.
A learner's content and language trajectories across a CLIL unit are worth reporting on separately, not combined into one blended grade.

v: 20 minutes to set up; brief notes each lesson
A two-strand tracking sheet per class

items: Choose two or three content outcomes and two or three language outcomes for the unit.
Design one small check for each outcome, spread across the lessons.
Record content and language results in separate columns.
At the end of the unit, write separate short comments on content and language for each learner.
Report the two strands separately, not as a single blended grade.
Share the tracking sheet with learners as a self-assessment checklist (Unit 42).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A tracking extract for one learner (written for this book):

lines: Content: explains two sources of the district’s water ✓; explains two causes of lake shrinkage ✓; evaluates two solutions (partly).
Language: uses cause-and-effect connectors ✓; uses the passive in describing processes (not yet); presents a recommendation clearly ✓.

blocks.x: Comment: Nandini understands the causes well and presents confidently. Next step: use the passive to describe processes (‘Water is pumped…’). A blended grade would hide the fact that her content is strong and her language is developing. This extends the dual-rubric principle of Unit 37 to the unit level.

body: Purpose: to show separate content and language tracking. Content: two parallel railway tracks, labelled ‘content’ and ‘language’, with a learner’s progress marked by stations along each. Style: clear, Indian railway theme. Board version: two parallel lines with dots.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a two-strand tracking sheet.

blocks.x: A class register with two narrow columns per outcome.

pts: A full CLIL unit benefits substantially from genuine collaboration between a language specialist and a subject specialist, where both exist.
Joint planning sessions, not just after-the-fact material sharing, produce the strongest integration of both aims.
Where one teacher fills both roles, protect distinct planning time for each dimension rather than blending the two into one rushed pass.

v: An English teacher and a subject teacher

items: Meeting 1: the subject teacher sets out content outcomes; the English teacher sets out language demands and opportunities.
Agree who teaches what, and where lessons will be shared.
Meeting 2: review draft materials together, checking accuracy of content and accessibility of language.
Meeting 3, after the unit: review results from both strands and agree changes.
Where one teacher fills both roles, plan the content and language dimensions in separate sessions, on separate days.
Use a cluster or DIET meeting to find a subject partner from another school.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Part of a planning conversation: A (science teacher): They must understand recharge. That’s the key concept. B (English teacher): Then they need the passive. ‘The groundwater is recharged by rain.’ I can teach that in my lesson before yours.

lines: A: Good. And I’ll use the same sentence on my diagram.
B: Can you check my simplified text? I’m not sure ‘aquifer’ is explained correctly.

blocks.x: Joint planning produces stronger integration than sharing materials after the event (Mehisto, Marsh and Frigols 2008).

body: Purpose: to show collaboration. Content: two teachers at a table, one with a science textbook and one with an English textbook, drawing on a shared plan with overlapping circles for content and language. Style: warm, realistic staff-room scene. Board version: two overlapping circles.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared planning sheet.

blocks.x: One planning sheet in a shared file in the staff room.

body: If time is short, protect the first meeting above all. Agreeing content outcomes and language demands at the start prevents most later problems.

points.h: Materials Development for a Full Unit
pts: Materials for a genuine CLIL unit typically can't simply be borrowed from a subject textbook or a language coursebook alone.
This extends Unit 37's materials-adaptation principle into original materials development, a considerably larger undertaking.
Build materials incrementally across a first run of the unit, refining based on what Unit 9's reflective practice reveals.

v: Across the first run of the unit
Subject textbook; open-licence resources; a materials log

items: Start with what exists: the subject textbook, government resources and local data.
For each lesson, adapt one key text by chunking, adding headings and visuals, and glossing terms (Unit 37).
Create task cards and organizers for each lesson.
After each lesson, note in a materials log what worked and what did not.
After the unit, revise the materials and store them where colleagues can use them.
Learners contribute photographs, interviews and maps.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A materials log entry (written for this book):

lines: Lesson 3, 12 Sept. Rainfall graph too detailed: learners spent 15 minutes reading years. Next time: show only 2000, 2010 and 2020. Interview task worked well; learners brought answers in Kannada and translated key sentences together.

blocks.x: Materials for a full CLIL unit rarely come ready-made. Building them across a first run and refining them through reflective practice (Unit 9) is more realistic than trying to write everything in advance. Unit 69 covers materials writing in depth.

body: Purpose: to show incremental materials development. Content: a folder shown three times, growing thicker, with sticky notes of revisions and a version label (first run, second run, shared). Style: clean, practical. Board version: three rectangles of increasing thickness.

items: DIKSHA (free, Government of India) for textbook-linked resources in several languages.
Google Drive (free) for storing and sharing the unit pack.

blocks.x: A box file in the staff room, with photocopy masters.

pts: Evaluate the unit against both content learning outcomes and language development outcomes, not a single blended judgement.
A unit that succeeds on content but stalls language development, or vice versa, needs a different fix than one failing on both.
This closes the loop with Unit 9's reflective practice, applied specifically to CLIL's dual-aim structure.

v: Tracking sheets; learner work; the materials log

items: Summarize the class results for content outcomes and language outcomes separately.
Place the unit in one of four quadrants: both strong, content strong only, language strong only, both weak.
For the quadrant, choose the matching fix (see model language).
Ask learners for feedback on what helped and what was difficult.
Revise the 4Cs grid and language map for the next run.
Review two units side by side.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Four quadrants and their fixes (written for this book):

lines: Content strong, language weak: add explicit language-for-learning frames and a language focus stage.
Language strong, content weak: the content may have been simplified too far; strengthen field-building with the subject teacher.
Both weak: the unit may be too demanding; reduce the scope or add more scaffolding early.
Both strong: raise cognitive demand, or hand more planning to learners.

blocks.x: Evaluating content and language separately shows which fix a unit needs. This closes the loop with the reflective practice of Unit 9.

body: Purpose: to show two-dimensional evaluation. Content: a two-by-two grid with axes ‘content outcomes’ and ‘language outcomes’; each quadrant has a short label and a small icon for its fix. Style: clear. Board version: a cross with four labels.

items: Google Forms (free) for learners’ end-of-unit feedback.

blocks.x: Paper feedback slips with two questions: what helped, what was hard.

body: Plan one six-lesson unit with a subject colleague using the 4Cs grid and a language map. After teaching it, place the unit in one of the four quadrants and make one change before the next run. Record both runs; the comparison is a small piece of action research (Unit 67).

dek: Unit 55 of 100: from Tier II's light-touch introduction to genuinely planning a sustained content-and-language-integrated unit, with the collaboration and assessment it demands.

aims.x: Unit 37 introduced CLIL through single lessons that taught a familiar topic from another subject through English. A single lesson proves the concept. A sustained content unit tests whether the approach can build both subject knowledge and language over several weeks. This unit takes one worked example, a six-lesson Class 8 unit on water management in the learners’ district, and follows it from choosing the content to evaluating the result.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: select content substantial and relevant enough to sustain a full CLIL unit;
map content, communication, cognition and culture lesson by lesson and spot uneven demand;
plan a scaffolding arc that reduces support across a unit;
map language of, for and through learning for a whole unit, while staying open to emerging language;
track and report content and language learning as separate strands;
plan jointly with a subject colleague, or protect separate planning time when teaching both;
develop and refine unit materials across a first run;
evaluate a unit against content and language outcomes separately and choose the right fix.

why: Why this matters. A single CLIL lesson proves the concept. A genuine content unit tests whether the methodology can sustain both content mastery and language development over time.

background.x: Content and Language Integrated Learning is usually defined as a dual-focused approach in which an additional language is used for the learning and teaching of both content and language (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010). Do Coyle’s 4Cs framework, of content, communication, cognition and culture, is the most widely used planning tool, and the language triptych of language of, for and through learning helps teachers anticipate the language a content unit will demand. Mehisto, Marsh and Frigols (2008) stress that sustained CLIL, with its demands for collaboration and materials, needs institutional support rather than individual enthusiasm alone.

Research on CLIL classrooms has produced mixed and carefully qualified findings. Christiane Dalton-Puffer (2007), studying Austrian classrooms, found gains in learners’ vocabulary and fluency, but also noted that classroom talk did not automatically develop the academic language functions, such as defining, explaining and hypothesizing, that subject learning needs. The lesson for planners is that language for thinking must be taught deliberately. Jim Cummins’s distinction between conversational fluency and academic language proficiency (Cummins 2000) explains why learners who chat easily in English may still struggle with a science explanation.

The Indian context is distinctive. Many learners already study science and social science in English, whether in English-medium schools or through a switch of medium at the upper primary or secondary stage. Much of this is content taught in English without planned language support. NEP 2020 recommends that, wherever possible, the medium of instruction until at least Grade 5, and preferably till Grade 8 and beyond, should be the home language, and it encourages bilingual teaching and learning materials (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). NCF 2023 also treats multilingualism as a resource (NCERT 2023). A well-planned CLIL unit fits these aims when it values the home language for understanding and uses English purposefully for the content, rather than replacing one with the other. Unit 71 returns to translanguaging in depth.

items: Content outcomes. Short checks within the unit and a final task that shows subject understanding, such as an explained diagram.
Language outcomes. Evidence of target language functions, such as cause and effect or recommending, assessed with a language rubric.
Final product. A group proposal presented to an audience, scored on separate content and language criteria.
Teacher portfolio. The 4Cs grid, language map, materials log and a two-dimension review.
Which subject topic in your school would sustain a full CLIL unit?
Where in your plans are cognition and language both high at the same moment?
How does your scaffolding change across a unit?
How do you report learners who are strong in content but weak in English, or the reverse?
Who could you plan a unit with, and when could you meet?
How are learners’ home languages used in your content lessons?

terms.def: A planning framework for CLIL that asks teachers to integrate content, communication, cognition and culture in each unit (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010); for example, a science lesson on the water cycle also plans its language and thinking demands.
A unit of work in which a subject topic, such as the water cycle, and the English needed to learn it are planned and taught together, using the 4Cs framework.
The level of thinking a task requires, from recalling and describing to analysing and evaluating; CLIL lessons plan the language needed for each level.
Planning in which a subject teacher and an English teacher work together to set content outcomes, language demands and support, as in content and language integrated learning.
In the CLIL Language Triptych, the language learners need to take part in learning, such as asking questions, working in groups and presenting (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).
In the CLIL Language Triptych, the subject-specific language needed to understand and express content, such as the terms for photosynthesis (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).
In the CLIL Language Triptych, the new language that emerges as learners think, discuss and learn content (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).
A teacher’s running record of the materials used or adapted for a unit, noting sources, changes made and how well they worked, so that the materials can be improved on the next run.

A planned reduction in support across a unit of work, from heavy scaffolding in early lessons to independent performance by the end. It makes the gradual handover of responsibility to learners visible in the unit plan.
Tracking two strands of learning, such as language and subject content, or process and product, side by side, often on a simple tracking sheet. It keeps both visible when judging learner progress.
